title: Oat milk bar soap
subtitle: A white, skin-softening bar for sensitive or dry skin
excerpt: Cold-process bar soap made with oat milk in place of water, giving the finished bar extra skin-softening properties from the beta-glucans and proteins in the oats. Made on olive, coconut, and sweet almond oil at a 6% superfat. Yields seven bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.
sourceNotes: Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997), liquid substitution in cold-process soap; milk soaps run hot due to milk sugars. Soap-Calc SAP values (accessed 2026): coconut 0.190, olive 0.134, sweet almond 0.136. Oat milk substitution: freeze to slush before adding lye, as with carrot juice, to prevent scorching. Beta-glucan in oats: skin-conditioning action documented in cosmetics literature; the concentration surviving the alkaline saponification process is debated but traditionally valued.

recipe.batchNotes: Milk sugars make the reaction run hot. Freeze the oat milk to slush before adding lye, work in short additions, and leave the mould uncovered if it runs very hot in the gel phase to prevent separation.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Oat milk bars cure in 4-6 weeks and keep up to 2 years if stored cool and dry.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: 2 years in a cool, dry place. Milk soaps can develop a slight cream-coloured surface over time, this is normal. Discard at any sign of orange spots (DOS) on the cut face or a rancid smell.

glossaryTerms.definition: The reaction between fat and sodium hydroxide that produces soap. When oat milk replaces water, the lye still dissolves into the liquid and the saponification proceeds in the same way, but the milk sugars make the exothermic reaction run hotter.
The point at which the blended soap batter holds a light trail drizzled on its surface, the signal to mould. Milk batters often trace faster than water-based batters.

The percentage of fat left unsaponified in the finished bar, contributing a conditioning quality. This recipe uses 6%, slightly higher than the standard 5%, to compensate for the alkaline environment reducing any residual oat protein benefit.

content.text: Oat milk soap is a cold-process bar made with oat milk in place of distilled water, giving a creamy white bar with a gentle, skin-softening quality. The oat proteins and beta-glucans that survive the alkaline process leave a mild, conditioning feel on the skin. Made on olive, coconut, and sweet almond oil at a 6% superfat. Seven bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.

items.prepNote: pure (not extra virgin); 50% of oil weight; conditioning base

content.text: Prepare the oat milk lye solution

Put on protective gloves and goggles. Freeze the oat milk to a slush in ice-cube trays, about 2 hours. The slush slows the reaction and prevents the milk sugars scorching and turning the batter orange.

Place the oat milk slush in the HDPE pitcher. Add the sodium hydroxide slowly, a tablespoon at a time, stirring between additions. The solution will turn yellow-orange as the sugars react with the lye, this is normal. Stir until fully dissolved. Cool to 38-42°C.
Melt the coconut oil, combine with olive and sweet almond oils, and bring to 38-42°C.
Pour the lye solution into the oils. Stick-blend in short bursts until the batter reaches light
. Milk batters can accelerate quickly, pour as soon as you hit light trace.
Pour into the mould. Leave the mould uncovered if it feels warm to the touch, milk soaps run hotter than water-based batters and benefit from more air circulation. Leave 24-48 hours.
Unmould when firm. Cut into 7 bars wearing gloves. Cure on a ventilated rack for 4-6 weeks. The
is complete when a corner touched to the tongue gives no zap.
Store cured bars on a ventilated rack in a cool, dry place. The bars may develop a slight creamy surface tinge as they age, a normal characteristic of milk soaps. The
keeps the bar conditioning for the full 2-year shelf life. Discard at any sign of orange spots (DOS) or a rancid smell.
